items.sx: Right face and arm weakness, leg mostly spared. Speech is slow, effortful and broken, but he understands everything.
items.why: Left frontal lobe: the lateral precentral gyrus (face and arm area of the motor homunculus) plus Broca's area in the left inferior frontal gyrus. Typical of a left MCA superior-division stroke. The leg area sits on the medial surface (ACA territory), so the leg is spared.

items.sx: Fluent speech full of made-up words, poor comprehension, can't repeat. No weakness. He doesn't realise anything is wrong.
items.why: Wernicke's area: posterior superior temporal gyrus of the dominant (usually left) hemisphere. Lesion = fluent receptive aphasia with poor insight. Left MCA inferior division.

items.sx: Left leg weak and numb, arm and face much less affected. He's also apathetic and has become incontinent of urine.
items.why: Right paracentral lobule (leg area of motor and sensory cortex on the medial surface), supplied by the right anterior cerebral artery. Frontal involvement causes abulia and loss of bladder control.

items.sx: She ignores the left side of the world: eats food from the right half of her plate, shaves only the right side, and denies her left arm is weak.
items.why: Right (non-dominant) parietal lobe. Hemineglect and anosognosia (denial of deficit) are classic right parietal signs, usually right MCA territory.

items.sx: Can't see the right half of the world with either eye (right homonymous hemianopia), but central vision is spared. No weakness.
items.why: Left occipital lobe (primary visual cortex), usually a left posterior cerebral artery stroke. Macular sparing happens because the occipital pole has dual supply from the MCA.

items.sx: Sudden weakness of the whole right side: face, arm and leg equally. No numbness, no speech, vision or thinking problems.
items.why: Posterior limb of the left internal capsule: a lacunar stroke. Corticospinal and corticobulbar fibres are packed tightly here, so a tiny infarct weakens face, arm and leg equally without cortical signs (pure motor stroke). Lenticulostriate arteries; linked to hypertension.

items.sx: Numbness of the whole left side of the body and face, with no weakness at all.
items.why: Right thalamus (ventral posterolateral and posteromedial nuclei): pure sensory lacunar stroke. All sensory pathways relay here before the cortex.

items.sx: Can't write, can't do simple math, mixes up left and right, and can't name his own fingers.
items.why: Gerstmann syndrome: left (dominant) angular gyrus in the inferior parietal lobule.

items.sx: Loss of fine touch and position sense in the left face and arm. With eyes closed she can't tell a key from a coin in her left hand.
items.why: Right postcentral gyrus (primary somatosensory cortex), face and arm area. Astereognosis means the cortical processing of touch is damaged.

items.sx: After a car crash his personality changed: impulsive, rude, poor planning, laughs at inappropriate times. Strength and sensation are normal.
items.why: Prefrontal cortex (often both frontal lobes; orbitofrontal contusions are common in crashes). Think Phineas Gage. Either side counts here.

items.sx: Right eye: droopy lid, dilated pupil, eye points down and out. Left arm and leg are weak.
items.why: Weber syndrome: right medial midbrain. The right CN III fascicles are hit (same-side eye findings) together with the right cerebral peduncle, whose corticospinal fibres haven't crossed yet (opposite-side weakness).

items.sx: Left eye can't look outward and the left face is weak (forehead included). Right arm and leg are weak.
items.why: Millard-Gubler syndrome: left caudal pons, ventral/medial. Left CN VI and CN VII (lower motor neuron, so the forehead is weak too) plus the left corticospinal tract (crosses below, so right-sided weakness).

items.sx: Vertigo, hoarse voice, trouble swallowing, right-sided Horner syndrome, right face loses pain and temperature, but on the body it's the LEFT side that lost pain and temperature. Right arm is clumsy.
items.why: Wallenberg (lateral medullary) syndrome on the right, usually a vertebral or PICA occlusion. Nucleus ambiguus (hoarse, dysphagia), spinal trigeminal nucleus (same-side face), spinothalamic tract (already crossed: opposite body), descending sympathetics (Horner), inferior cerebellar peduncle (ataxia). Strength is spared.

items.sx: Tongue sticks out and deviates to the left. Right arm and leg are weak, and he can't feel vibration or position in his right limbs.
items.why: Medial medullary (Dejerine) syndrome on the left: left CN XII nucleus or fibres (tongue points toward the lesion), left pyramid (crosses below: right weakness), left medial lemniscus (already crossed: right vibration/position loss). Anterior spinal artery.

items.sx: Sudden vertigo, left ear goes deaf, left face paralysed and numb to pain, and the right side of the body loses pain and temperature.
items.why: Lateral pontine syndrome on the left (AICA). Vestibular and cochlear nuclei, facial nucleus, spinal trigeminal nucleus and the already-crossed spinothalamic tract.

items.sx: Fully awake and aware but can't move anything: no arms, legs, face or speech. Can only blink and look up and down.
items.why: Locked-in syndrome: ventral pons on both sides (basilar artery occlusion). Corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts are cut, but the reticular activating system (consciousness) and vertical gaze centres in the midbrain are spared. Either side counts.

items.sx: Wide-based drunken-looking walk and can't sit up straight unsupported, but finger-to-nose and heel-to-shin are normal.
items.why: Cerebellar vermis (midline). It controls the trunk and gait. Classic in chronic alcohol damage and in childhood medulloblastoma.

items.sx: Right hand overshoots when reaching (dysmetria), tremor gets worse as the finger nears the target, and she sways and falls to the right.
items.why: Right cerebellar hemisphere. Cerebellar signs are on the SAME side as the lesion, because the cerebellar pathways cross twice.

items.sx: Both legs weak and stiff with brisk reflexes, numb from the belly button down, and he can't empty his bladder.
items.why: Complete thoracic cord lesion around T10 (the umbilicus dermatome), so the T7–T12 segment, both halves. Upper motor neuron signs below, a sensory level, and bladder failure.

items.sx: Stabbed in the back. Right leg is weak and has lost vibration and position sense; the LEFT leg has lost pain and temperature. Level around T10.
items.why: Brown-Séquard (right hemisection) at T7–T12. Corticospinal tract and dorsal columns haven't crossed yet (same side), while spinothalamic fibres crossed within 1–2 segments of entry (opposite side).

items.sx: Older man fell forward and hit his chin. His arms and hands are much weaker than his legs, with a cape-like loss of pain over the shoulders.
items.why: Central cord syndrome in the lower cervical cord (C5–C8). Arm fibres sit closest to the centre of the corticospinal tract, and crossing pain fibres in the centre get damaged first. Either half counts.

items.sx: After a diving accident he can't move arms or legs and can't breathe on his own.
items.why: High cervical cord, C1–C4. 'C3, 4, 5 keeps the diaphragm alive': the phrenic nerve comes from C3–C5, so a lesion here stops breathing. Either half counts.

items.sx: Numbness in the saddle area, weak legs with absent ankle reflexes (floppy, not stiff), and urinary retention after a huge disc herniation.
items.why: Cauda equina: the nerve roots below the end of the cord (L2 down). Root damage gives LOWER motor neuron signs. A surgical emergency.

items.sx: Can't see the upper right quarter of the world in either eye ('pie in the sky').
items.why: Left temporal lobe: Meyer's loop of the optic radiation (carrying upper-field fibres) dips into the temporal lobe.

items.sx: Can't see the lower left quarter of the world in either eye ('pie on the floor').
items.why: Right parietal lobe: the upper part of the optic radiation (Baum's loop, carrying lower-field fibres) runs through the parietal lobe.

items.sx: Slow, stiff and shuffling, with a pill-rolling tremor of the right hand at rest.
items.why: Substantia nigra pars compacta in the midbrain (more on the left for right-sided signs), whose dopamine neurons project to the striatum (putamen and caudate). Parkinson disease. Midbrain or putamen counts.

items.sx: Fluent speech and good comprehension, but she can't repeat a sentence back to you.
items.why: Conduction aphasia: arcuate fasciculus, the white-matter tract linking Wernicke's and Broca's areas, often damaged under the left supramarginal gyrus (inferior parietal).

items.sx: Left face, arm and leg weak, can't see the left half of the world, and ignores his left side. Eyes deviate to the right.
items.why: Large right MCA stroke: right frontal and parietal cortex. Eyes look toward the lesion because the right frontal eye field is out and the left one pushes the eyes right.

items.sx: Neither eye can look to the right, and the right side of the face is weak.
items.why: Right dorsal caudal pons: the abducens nucleus (horizontal gaze centre for both eyes via the MLF) with the facial nerve fibres looping around it (facial colliculus).

items.sx: A 26-year-old with MS: when she looks to the right, her left eye won't move inward and her right eye jerks (nystagmus). Convergence is normal.
items.why: Left medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) in the dorsomedial pons/midbrain: internuclear ophthalmoplegia. The MLF carries the signal from the right abducens nucleus to the left oculomotor nucleus. Bilateral INO in a young person suggests MS.

items.sx: After a stroke, the left side felt numb. Weeks later the same side burns with pain from light touch.
items.why: Right thalamus: Dejerine-Roussy (thalamic pain) syndrome, a central pain after a thalamic infarct.

items.sx: She can write a sentence but can't read it back. Right homonymous hemianopia.
items.why: Alexia without agraphia: left occipital lobe plus the splenium of the corpus callosum (left PCA). Words seen by the intact right visual cortex can't reach the left language areas.

items.sx: Both legs paralysed and lost pain and temperature below the belly button after aortic surgery, but vibration and position sense are normal.
items.why: Anterior cord syndrome at T7–T12 (anterior spinal artery infarct; the artery of Adamkiewicz can be hit in aortic surgery). The dorsal columns, supplied by the posterior spinal arteries, are spared.

items.sx: Bilateral leg weakness with brisk reflexes and a sensory level at the nipples.
items.why: Upper thoracic cord, T1–T6 (the nipple line is T4). Either half counts.

items.sx: Sudden right-sided weakness of the face and hand with slurred speech and clumsiness. No sensory loss, no aphasia.
items.why: Dysarthria-clumsy hand lacunar syndrome: genu/posterior limb of the left internal capsule or the left basis pontis.

items.sx: Loses vibration and position sense in both legs, falls when he closes his eyes in the shower. Low vitamin B12.
items.why: Subacute combined degeneration: dorsal columns (and lateral corticospinal tracts) along the cervical and thoracic cord. Positive Romberg = proprioceptive ataxia. Any cord segment counts.
